intro: Bad english translations often arise from raw machine output that misses context, nuance, or industry-specific terminology. Professional translators handle this through machine translation post-editing, or MTPE, to bring quality up to human standards while maintaining speed.

blocks.text: Why bad english translations happen in automated workflows

Machine translation engines operate on probability, not understanding. When you encounter bad english translations, it is usually because the engine failed to map the source language to a natural english equivalent. Common issues include literal translations of idioms, incorrect gender agreement, or a lack of awareness regarding the intended audience. These errors occur because the engine lacks the cultural context a human translator brings to a project.
The hidden costs of poor machine output

The cost of bad english translations is not just the time spent fixing them. It is also the mental tax on the translator. When you edit poor machine output, your brain works harder to ignore the errors while trying to construct the correct meaning. This process is known as cognitive load. If the time to edit exceeds 30 to 40 percent of the time it would take to translate the same text from scratch, the financial benefit of using machine translation vanishes. You end up with a higher risk of burnout and a lower quality final product.

items: Pre-scan the machine output for patterns of failure before you begin the full edit.
Use a translation management system that flags low-confidence segments.
Stop editing if you find yourself rewriting every sentence, as it is likely faster to start over.
Keep a personal termbase to ensure consistent terminology across all your projects.
Use keyboard shortcuts for common editing actions to reduce physical strain.

faq.question: Is post-editing always faster than human translation?
faq.answer: Not always. Studies show it can be 66 percent faster on average, but this depends heavily on the language pair and the quality of the initial machine output.

faq.question: How do I avoid over-editing?
faq.answer: Focus on accuracy and readability. If a sentence is grammatically correct and conveys the right meaning, leave it alone, even if you would have chosen a different stylistic approach.

faq.question: Does Lazur work with my CAT tools?
faq.answer: Lazur works with any app on your Mac. You can use it to dictate text or ask questions while your CAT tool is open in the background.

costs.title: Cognitive load
costs.text: The mental effort required to identify and fix errors in machine-generated text leads to faster fatigue.

costs.title: Time inefficiency
costs.text: Poor machine output forces you to perform a full retranslation, consuming more time than starting fresh.

costs.title: Quality risk
costs.text: Fatigue from editing poor quality text increases the likelihood of missing subtle errors in the final document.

causes.title: Lack of cultural context
causes.text: Machine engines lack the nuance required to correctly translate idioms and cultural references.

causes.title: Probability-based output
causes.text: Engines choose the most statistically likely word rather than the most accurate one for a specific context.

causes.title: Inconsistent terminology
causes.text: Without a linked termbase, engines often use different words for the same concept within one document.

fixes.title: Perform a quick scan
fixes.text: Before starting, read the first few paragraphs to assess the quality of the machine output.

fixes.title: Use a termbase
fixes.text: Ensure consistent terminology by maintaining a list of approved translations for key terms.

fixes.title: Avoid over-editing
fixes.text: Do not change stylistic choices if the original machine output is accurate and readable.
